title: Why We Must Cease Evil and Practice Good
author: Mingde
excerpt: The Buddha said: “Evil brings evil retribution; good brings good reward.”

inline.s: The Buddha said: “Evil brings evil retribution; good brings good reward.”
Question: What significance does ceasing evil and practicing good hold for Buddhist practice?

Answer: It holds tremendous significance. The heart of ceasing evil and practicing good is this: follow the principle of Heaven and cast out selfish desire. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Final Teaching, the Buddha said:
“You monks, who are now able to abide in the precepts, should restrain the five sense-faculties and not let them run loose, giving entrance to the five desires.”
In the Sutra in Forty-Two Sections, the Buddha said:
“One who pursues the Way is like one draped in dry grass
(that is, like one whose body is wrapped in dry grass)
—when fire comes he must flee it. When a follower of the Way sees desire, he must keep far from it.”

Therefore, faith in cause and effect, following the principle of Heaven, and casting out selfish desire—these are the foundation of Buddhist practice. For this reason Master Yinguang spared no effort in expounding the ceasing of evil and the practice of good, as can be seen throughout his Collected Writings.

[The five sense-faculties] are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. [The five desires] are craving for form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful sights; sound to pleasing voices and pleasant words; fragrance to sweet scents; taste to delicious flavors; and touch to agreeable tactile pleasures. Because these five can give rise to the mind of greed, they are called the five desires. To keep the precepts purely is to be able to control the five sense-faculties and remain unmoved by the five desires.
For students of the Pure Land school, the Buddha said in the Amitābha Sutra:
“One cannot be born in that land with but few roots of goodness, blessings, and virtue, or few causal conditions.”

The vow among the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice in Pure Land is: to feel revulsion for this Sahā world and to yearn for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, one is required at the time of death to keep right mindfulness clear and distinct
(the ten successive recitations at the point of death; for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth

. Think about it: if selfish desire is ordinarily in command, where are roots of goodness and blessings to come from? How can one speak of revulsion for the Sahā world? And at the point of death can one keep right mindfulness clear and distinct
(the ten successive recitations at the point of death)
[Roots of goodness] are the good deeds of body, speech, and mind; because they can bring forth wondrous fruits, they are called roots of goodness.

For students of the Chan (Zen) school, one must attain selflessness and freedom from thought. If selfish desire is ordinarily in command, can one be selfless and free from thought? One would surely be speaking of emptiness with every word while treading on existence with every step.
Therefore Master Yinguang said:
“The single principle of cause and effect is the great smelting furnace by which the sages of this world and of the world beyond
(that is, of the mundane and the supramundane)

refine the ordinary into sages. If from the very first one does not investigate cause and effect, then even after mastering both the school and the teachings, one may still err in matters of cause and effect. Once cause and effect are mistaken, one has a share in falling and no means of rising. Do not say this principle is shallow and so disregard it: the Tathagata’s attainment of perfect enlightenment and beings’ descent into the three evil paths—neither falls outside of cause and effect. Ordinary people’s minds are small; wherever the sutras speak of the great workings of cause and effect they may fail to grasp them, so one should use the shallower and more accessible things of this world as a means of entering the sublime. Such as the Record of Hidden Merits by Wenchang
(that is, The Record of Hidden Merits by Emperor Wenchang)
and the Treatise on Response and Retribution of the Most High, so that one may
(that is, “so that”)
read them thoroughly, examine them carefully, and put them into practice—then every person may become a good citizen, and every person may end birth and death.”
(from A Reply to Layman Xie Chengming of Sichuan) Please pay special attention to the phrase “every person may end birth and death.”

[This world and the world beyond] refers to the mundane world and the supramundane world. The mundane world is the world of living beings; the supramundane world is the world of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

means “hidden merit”
Question: Above we spoke of “casting out selfish desire”—is this not asceticism?
Answer: First, we must understand the reason why selfish desire should be cast out. Confucius said:
“Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.”

(translated: what you yourself do not wish for, do not impose on others.) Why should we “not impose on others what we ourselves do not desire”? Apart from the fact that morality, conscience, and even the law require us to act this way, there is a deeper reason: “Whatever you send out will all come back to you”—this is a law of the universe. Just like the law of action and reaction in physics, wherever there is an action there is necessarily a reaction; you push against a wall, and the wall pushes back against you. Whatever you send out, that is what you will receive. When you do evil, evil will be visited upon you; when you speak evil words, evil words will be visited upon you; when you harbor evil thoughts, evil thoughts will be visited upon you. Conversely, when you do good, good will be visited upon you; when you speak good words, good words will be visited upon you; when you harbor good thoughts, good thoughts will be visited upon you. This is a law of the universe!

There is an idiom called “inviting the gentleman into the jar” (qing jun ru weng), which comes from the story of Zhou Xing, a cruel official under Empress Wu Zetian. Someone secretly reported that Zhou Xing and Qiu Shenji (jì) had conspired to rebel, so Empress Wu ordered Lai Junchen to try the case. Thereupon Lai Junchen invited Zhou Xing to his home as a guest, and as they drank wine together they discussed certain cases. Lai Junchen said to Zhou Xing: “There are some prisoners who, after being interrogated again and again, still refuse to confess their crimes. What method is there to make them confess?” Zhou Xing said: “That is easy! Just take a jar, heat it by burning charcoal all around it, and then have the prisoner climb into the jar—what crime would he dare not confess?” Lai Junchen then ordered his attendants to fetch a jar, and, following Zhou Xing’s method, heated it with burning charcoal all around. Then Lai Junchen stood up and said to Zhou Xing: “Someone has accused you of plotting rebellion. Her Majesty the Empress Dowager has ordered me to interrogate you, so please climb into this jar yourself, old friend (inviting the gentleman into the jar)!” Zhou Xing was utterly terrified, and at once kowtowed and confessed his crimes.
The great judge of the universe is the same way: for those who do evil, he will in every case “invite the gentleman into the jar.” Therefore, in the Buddha Pitaka Sutra, the Buddha said:
“Evil brings evil retribution.”

This means that where there is an evil cause, there will surely be an evil result. The wise fear the cause, knowing that creating a cause will surely bring its result; the foolish fear the result, because they do not believe in the law of cause and effect, or are unwilling to believe in it, and so create causes without any restraint—yet when calamity arrives, they panic and blame heaven and earth, never thinking to blame themselves.

Whatever you send out will all come back to you”—this law of the universe applies equally to those of good mind, good speech, and good deeds. Therefore, immediately after the Buddha said “evil brings evil retribution,” he went on to say:
“Good brings good reward.”
“Evil brings evil retribution; good brings good reward”—this is the cosmic law of cause and effect, also called karmic retribution.

The people of the world are all “near-sighted”: they see only the present, not knowing that there is a future, and even less knowing that there are future lives. They are like the cicada, which enjoys only the summer and does not know that autumn and winter will follow in succession!
In philosophy there is a famous saying:
Freedom is the recognition of necessity.

Ordinary people suppose that freedom is doing whatever one pleases, forgetting that this “whatever one pleases” is itself the creation of a cause, which will inevitably be repaid with a result. If you have the freedom to jump from a building, you have the freedom to break your leg; if you have the freedom to eat and drink to excess, you have the freedom to be beset by illness; such a cause, such a fruit. Therefore the wise understand that only through a deep recognition of necessity (karmic retribution) can one attain true freedom. If you wish for the fruit of gaining blessings and avoiding calamity, you must create the cause of gaining blessings and avoiding calamity. If you wish for the fruit of health, happiness, and longevity, you must create the cause of health, happiness, and longevity.

The above has been said with regard to worldly dharmas. The goal of Buddhist practitioners is to transcend the world—to leave the three realms and end birth and death. In the Pure Land school, one must recite the Buddha’s name and at the time of death keep right mindfulness clear and distinct (the ten successive recitations at the point of death); in the Chan school, one must practice until the ten thousand thoughts return to one, and the one returns to nothing, thereby seeing one’s true nature. Therefore, besides cultivating the power of concentration, one must also pare away the entangling forces of the dusty world. The mind is like a horse: if it is a tamed horse, a mere tug on the reins keeps it from straying, and it may even know of itself to walk the straight path. But if it is an untamed horse, you must constantly pull the reins tight (the power of concentration) to master it; once its wild nature erupts, you may not be able to hold it at all! Casting out selfish desire is precisely paring away the entangling forces of the dusty world, so that one’s practice gains strength and at the time of death right mindfulness is clear and distinct—ensuring the end of birth and death and departure from the three realms.
After reading all of the above, would you still consider casting out selfish desire to be ignorance, superstition, or so-called “asceticism”?
